report.source_text: The patient has been recovering gradually without the use of any intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis and was discharged home to continue therapy in the community. He was seen in an outpatient clinic to assess his condition a few months postdischarge. Here he was found to have improved significantly. Normal power noted during the follow-up with good reflexes recovery. Now, he is able to walk independently. However, he still is not yet back to baseline—becoming tired more easily than usual with mild manageable backpain.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 9-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 3-week history of progressive atraumatic back pain, unsteadiness requiring assistance with walking and dressing, and lower limb weakness. On neurological examination, he demonstrated significant areflexia in both lower limbs (absent left leg reflexes, barely elicitable right leg reflexes) with preserved upper limb reflexes and normal sensory examination, consistent with a lower limb-predominant pattern. MRI with contrast revealed symmetrical enhancement of the cauda equina and proximal mastoid segments of the facial nerves. Clinical assessment documented albuminocytological dissociation in cerebrospinal fluid. The patient tested positive for COVID-19 on admission nasopharyngeal swab, representing a potential preceding viral trigger. He was managed conservatively without immunoglobulin therapy, with analgesics, gabapentin, and physiotherapy. His disability grade remained static (2-3) during admission and he improved gradually. At follow-up a few months post-discharge, he demonstrated significant recovery with normalized power, good reflex recovery, and independent ambulation, though not yet fully back to baseline.
